newsitem.title: CHINA: China says it will talk human rights with any group.
newsitem.headline: China says it will talk human rights with any group.

text.p: China is ready to hold talks on human rights with any group as long as those discussions are based on mutual respect and equality, one of China's top human rights officials said on Wednesday.

Zhu Muzhi, speaking on state television after his return from a visit to Europe that included Italy, Spain and Norway, said he expected an end to international differences over human rights even though disputes could not be ironed out overnight.

"We will maintain that as long as all parties have an attitude of mutual respect and equality, we would like to hold a dialogue with any organisations and individuals," Zhu, president of the non-governmental China Society for the Study of Human Rights, was quoted by state television as saying.

Zhu's visit to Norway last month included the first meeting between Chinese officials and representatives of the London-based human rights group Amnesty International, one of the sternest critics of China's human rights record.

"Through the visit, we found that more and more people recognise that there are many ways to make gains in human rights," Zhu was quoted as saying. "This trend brings about good prospects for ironing out differences on human rights.

"International differences on human rights clearly cannot be resolved overnight," he added. "But dialogue will eventually prevail over confrontation, paving the way for a correct resolution of differences on the issue of human rights."

The Amnesty International meeting with Zhu, a former minister of culture and education, marked the first time international human rights activists had won access to such a senior member of the Chinese hierarchy.
Beijing frequently comes under fire from Western governments and human rights watchdogs for its heavy-handed treatment of political dissidents.

China rejects such criticism of its human rights record as interference in its internal affairs, arguing that ensuring adequate food and clothing for its 1.2 billion people is more important than political freedoms.
China's small circle of active dissidents has dwindled in recent years, with most activists fleeing into exile or now serving lengthy jail terms.
China last week released two dissidents jailed for their role in the student-led 1989 pro-democracy campaign after an appeals court quashed their convictions.
It was the first time a Chinese court had overturned sentences meted out to activists involved in the protests that were crushed by the military on June 4, 1989 with heavy loss of life.
